title: US lawmakers criticize Nigerian government's handling of insecurity at congressional briefing - Ocean County Leader
text:
US lawmakers have criticized the Nigerian government for its response to ongoing insecurity and violence in the country. The comments were made during a joint briefing of the United States House Appropriations Committee focused on alleged persecution of Christians in Nigeria.
Congressman Chris Smith, who represents New Jersey’s 4th district in Congress and has served since 1981, addressed the issue at the event. “The Nigerian government has a fundamental, constitutional obligation to protect its citizens; however, the perpetrators of this persecution operate with complete impunity,” Smith said.
Smith, who is also Chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Africa Subcommittee, stated that the US would hold Nigeria accountable for these killings. “The Nigerian government is trying to run out the clock; we cannot allow this to happen. We must act quickly and decisively to save more lives,” he added.
These remarks came after President Donald Trump designated Nigeria as a country of particular concern (CPC) due to religious freedom violations and threatened military action if conditions did not improve. Trump first placed Nigeria on the CPC list in 2020, but it was removed by President Joe Biden before being redesignated by Trump on October 31. Trump also warned that US aid could be halted if steps were not taken against Christian persecution.
Rep. Brian Mast supported Trump’s decision regarding Nigeria’s status as a CPC. He said, “The US must demand that the Nigerian government disarm these militias, return displaced families to their homes, and bring the perpetrators to justice.”
Riley Moore, Vice Chair of the House Appropriations Legislative Branch Subcommittee and an advocate for religious liberty, reinforced concerns about Christian persecution in Nigeria: “The world will no longer turn a blind eye to the persecution of Christians in Nigeria.”
Vicky Hartzler, Chair of the U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom, commented on insufficient responses from Nigerian authorities despite early warnings about attacks: “Resources could also be invested in using early warning systems to reduce community violence, and the U.S. government should insist that Nigerian government officials respond when there is an early warning.
“Too many times, local villagers learn of an impending attack and reach out for protection, only to have their cries for help ignored to their ultimate demise. Worse yet, there are stories of law enforcement being called during an attack, and yet no help is sent. This is unacceptable!”
Ebenezer Obadare from the Council on Foreign Relations attributed much of Nigeria’s insecurity to jihadist groups such as Boko Haram. He noted that recent US actions had increased pressure on Nigeria’s government: “Washington must keep up the pressure. The policy goal should be two-fold: first, work with the Nigerian military to neutralize Boko Haram.
“Second, the United States should put pressure on President Tinubu to (1) make Sharia law unconstitutional in the twelve northern states where they has been adopted since 2000 and (2) disband the various Hisbah groups across northern states seeking to enforce and impose Islamic law on all citizens regardless of their religious identity.”
A congressional hearing was also held November 20 examining escalating violence in Nigeria following Trump’s declaration.
Chris Smith was born in Rahway, New Jersey in 1953 and currently resides in Manchester Township. He graduated from The College of New Jersey with a BS degree in 1975.https://www.channelstv.com/2025/12/02/insecurity-us-lawmakers-accuse-nigerian-government-of-failing-to-stop-killings/
